title: Ship it, it's only three points
scenario: A support-agent team rewrote its prompt to improve partial refunds. They ran both suites once and wrote a note recommending release. You review the numbers before anyone clicks deploy (exhibit).
exhibit:
(made-up example data)

RUN: prompt v7 vs v6, 1 trial per task
  capability suite, partial refunds:   30% -> 52%
  regression suite, 120 tasks:         100% -> 97%   (4 tasks newly failing)
  cost per task:                       $0.04 -> $0.09
  model setting:                       "support-model-latest" (alias)

TASK cancel-order-31
  per-trial success rate: about 80%
  customers need it to work every time

TEAM NOTE
  "Capability is up 22 points. Regression is only 3 points down. Ship it."

questions.prompt: The regression suite fell from 100% to 97%. How should the team read this?

options.text: It is normal noise, so a 3-point drop on a regression suite is fine.
options.explanation: Anthropic says regression evals should have a nearly 100% pass rate, and a drop means something is broken. Noise is possible with one trial, but the answer is more trials and a look at the 4 tasks, not a shrug.

options.text: The capability gain cancels the drop, so the net result is positive.
options.explanation: The two suites answer different questions. A gain on new skills does not pay for breaking old ones.

options.text: Something broke. Look at the 4 tasks that now fail before release.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic: regression evals should pass at nearly 100%, and a drop signals that something is broken. Run more trials to confirm, then fix.

options.text: The 4 tasks are too hard, so move them to the capability suite.
options.explanation: Tasks graduate from capability to regression when they pass reliably. Moving failing tasks the other way just hides a regression.

questions.prompt: Cost per task went from $0.04 to $0.09. What should the team do with this number?

options.text: Ignore it. Cost is a billing matter, not an eval matter.
options.explanation: Anthropic says evals give you baselines for latency, token usage, cost per task and error rates, so cost belongs in the eval run.

options.text: Keep it as a baseline next to quality and compare it on every run.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic lists cost per task and latency as things you can track on a fixed bank of tasks. A doubled cost is a change worth catching.

options.text: Accept it, since quality is the only thing a regression suite tracks.
options.explanation: A suite can track more than quality. Anthropic names latency, token usage, cost and error rates as free baselines.

options.text: Wait for the monthly invoice, which is more exact than any eval.
options.explanation: An invoice arrives after release. A baseline in the eval run shows the change before users see it.

questions.prompt: The model setting is a `latest` alias. What do the vendor docs support?

options.text: Pin a specific version, and run the suite before any upgrade.
options.explanation: Right. Claude model IDs stay constant, OpenAI snapshots lock a version, and Gemini says most production apps should use a specific stable model. Treat an upgrade as a change and test it.

options.text: Keep the alias, because the vendor tests every update on your tasks.
options.explanation: Vendors cannot test your tasks. Gemini says a `latest` alias is hot-swapped with each new release.

options.text: Pin the model, then skip the suite, since a pinned model cannot change.
options.explanation: The Claude docs say infrastructure updates can still cause minor differences in behavior. The suite is how you notice.

options.text: Move to the newest preview model, because previews are the most stable.
options.explanation: Gemini says preview models are deprecated with at least 2 weeks notice. A stable model is the one the docs advise for production.

questions.prompt: Customers need cancel-order-31 to work every time. About 80% of trials pass. What is pass^3?

options.text: About 99%, because at least one of three trials passes.
options.explanation: That is pass@3: at least one success in k trials. It rises with k, and it does not show whether the task works every time.

options.text: About 80%, because pass^3 is the average of the three trials.
options.explanation: pass^3 is not an average. It needs all three trials to pass, so the chances multiply and the number falls.

options.text: About 64%, because only the first two trials matter.
options.explanation: pass^3 needs all three trials to succeed, so the third counts too.

options.text: About 51%: 0.8 x 0.8 x 0.8 is the chance all three pass.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's example is the same: 75% per trial gives about 42% for pass^3. This metric matters when users expect reliable behavior every time.
